authoring.value:
First, we find the first-order derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({z}^{2}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}-\frac{3}{\operatorname{ln}⁡z}) \\  & =3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we find ${f}_{xy}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{x}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xy}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({f}_{x}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(3{x}^{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}) \\  & =6{x}^{2}y{z}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we find ${f}_{xyz}(x,y,z)$ by differentiating ${f}_{xy}(x,y,z)$ with respect to $z:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyz}(x,y,z) & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({f}_{xy}(x,y,z)) \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(6{x}^{2}y{z}^{2}) \\  & =12{x}^{2}yz\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we evaluate ${f}_{xyz}(x,y,z)$ at $(-1,2,1):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{xyz}(-1,2,1) & =12(-1)^{2}(2)(1)=24\end{aligned}
$$

Domain clarification: the original function is undefined at $z=1$, since $\ln1=0$. Consequently the literal value $f_{xyz}(-1,2,1)$ in the source prompt is undefined. The derivatives above are valid on $z>0$, $z\ne1$; there $f_x=3x^2y^2z^2$, $f_{xy}=6x^2yz^2$, and $f_{xyz}=12x^2yz$. Thus $f_{xyz}(-1,2,z)=24z$ and
$$\lim_{z\to1,\ z\ne1}f_{xyz}(-1,2,z)=24.$$
The clarified study question explicitly asks for this limit, or continuous extension of the derivative, so the source's accepted answer $24$ and all original choices remain valid. This extension does not define the original function or its literal derivative at the excluded point.
